course.title: World Literature: A Global Survey
course.description: A guided tour of the stories, poems, and plays that cultures around the world have treasured, from ancient Mesopotamia to the twentieth century. You will learn to read across traditions, compare works thoughtfully, and see shared human themes carried by very different voices. Topic structure is adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

lessons.title: Diagnostic: what do you already know?

questions.prompt: Which of these is the oldest surviving great epic, written in ancient Mesopotamia?
questions.explanation: The Epic of Gilgamesh, about the king of Uruk, predates the Greek epics by well over a thousand years.

questions.prompt: Homer is traditionally credited with which two epics?
questions.explanation: The Iliad tells of the Trojan War; the Odyssey follows Odysseus home to Ithaca.

questions.prompt: The Tale of Genji, an early masterpiece often called the world's first novel, was written by whom?
questions.explanation: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady of the Heian court, composed it in Japan around the eleventh century.

questions.prompt: Dante Alighieri's great poem of hell, purgatory, and paradise is called the?
questions.explanation: The Divine Comedy guides the reader through the three realms of the afterlife, with Virgil and Beatrice as guides.

questions.prompt: In which collection does Scheherazade tell stories night after night to save her life?
questions.explanation: The Thousand and One Nights uses a frame story in which the queen spins tales such as Sindbad and Aladdin.

questions.prompt: Which novel, centered on Okonkwo and the Igbo world, is a landmark of African literature?
questions.explanation: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) portrays Igbo life on the eve of colonial disruption.

questions.prompt: The style called magical realism is most associated with which author of One Hundred Years of Solitude?
questions.explanation: Garcia Marquez wove the marvelous into everyday life in the town of Macondo.

questions.prompt: Reading 'across cultures' in world literature mainly means?
options: judging every work by one culture's standards
reading only in the original languages
comparing works from different traditions while respecting each context
questions.explanation: The aim is thoughtful comparison that keeps each work's own world in view.

lessons.title: What is world literature, and how do we read across cultures?
lessons.grammar_note: Italicize the titles of long works such as novels and epics; put the titles of short poems and single stories in quotation marks.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to say what people mean by world literature, explain why it is more than a list of famous books, and name the habits of mind that let a reader move between very different traditions. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you met works from Mesopotamia, Greece, Japan, Italy, the Arab world, Africa, and Latin America. What do you think lets us read them side by side at all? Hold onto your answer; we will sharpen it as we go.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: World literature is the body of literary works that circulate beyond their home culture and are read, translated, and valued around the globe. The phrase goes back to Goethe, who spoke of a coming age in which national literatures would meet and enrich one another. Reading across cultures does not mean flattening differences or ranking every book against one tradition. It means approaching a text with curiosity about its own time, place, language, and values, while also noticing the human concerns it shares with works from far away. Most of us meet these works in translation, so part of reading well is remembering that a translator has made choices, and that a poem or story may carry meanings its first audience felt but we must learn. Good readers ask three questions: what is this work doing on its own terms, what does it have in common with others, and what does comparison reveal that reading alone would miss?

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe coined the term Weltliteratur in the 1820s, imagining a conversation among the literatures of the world. The survey ahead ranges widely: the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh, Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, India's Ramayana and Mahabharata, the Chinese Tang poets Li Bai and Du Fu, Japan's Tale of Genji, Dante's Divine Comedy, the Arabic Thousand and One Nights, Cervantes' Don Quixote, Shakespeare's plays, the great realist novels of Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, and Flaubert, the modern visions of Kafka and Borges, and twentieth-century voices such as Achebe, Garcia Marquez, Mahfouz, and Tagore. These are not the only important works, but they are widely taught and translated, which makes them useful shared ground. As you meet each one, notice both what is strange and what feels familiar.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check yourself. 1) In one sentence, define world literature. 2) Who coined the term Weltliteratur? 3) Name two of the three questions a careful cross-cultural reader asks. 4) True or false: reading across cultures means judging all works by a single standard. 5) Why does translation matter when we read world literature? Answers: 1) The literary works that travel beyond their home culture to be read and valued worldwide. 2) Goethe. 3) Any two of: what is this work doing on its own terms; what does it share with others; what does comparison reveal. 4) False; it means comparing while respecting each context. 5) Because most readers meet these works in translation, and a translator's choices shape the meaning we receive.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming an older or foreign work is simpler than a modern one; ancient epics are often formally sophisticated. Mistake: treating translation as a transparent window rather than an act of interpretation. Mistake: using one culture's taste as the measuring stick for all others. Exit ticket: (a) What is the single best short definition of world literature? (b) Name one reason translation deserves a reader's attention. Answers: (a) literature that circulates and is valued beyond its culture of origin; (b) because a translator makes choices that affect tone, meaning, and nuance, so we are always reading a version, not the untouched original.

lessons.title: The ancient world: Gilgamesh, Homer, and the Bible as literature
lessons.grammar_note: An epic is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds; keep the word for that form and do not use it loosely to mean any long book.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe three foundational ancient traditions, name their central works and figures, and explain what it means to read a sacred text 'as literature.' Warm-up: in the diagnostic you identified the oldest surviving epic. Why might the age of a work make it more interesting rather than less? Think about how many later stories may echo it before you read on.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The ancient world gave later writers many of their deepest patterns. The Epic of Gilgamesh, set in Mesopotamia, follows a powerful but restless king whose friendship with the wild man Enkidu, and his grief at Enkidu's death, send him searching for immortality he cannot keep. Homer's Iliad concentrates on the rage of Achilles during the Trojan War, while the Odyssey traces Odysseus' long, trick-filled journey home. To read the Bible 'as literature' is to attend to its narrative craft, poetry, and imagery, such as the drama of Genesis, the laments of Job, the songs of the Psalms, and the love poetry of the Song of Songs, without reducing the reading to a question of belief. Across these traditions we already see themes that will recur throughout the course: mortality and the wish to escape it, the pull of home, the testing of a hero, and the bond between companions.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: The Epic of Gilgamesh survives on clay tablets in Sumerian and Akkadian; its flood story, told by the survivor Utnapishtim, strikingly parallels later flood narratives. Homer, traditionally a single Greek poet, is credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, composed from an oral tradition and foundational to Western literature. The Hebrew Bible, gathered over centuries, contains history, law, prophecy, proverb, and some of the most influential poetry ever written; read as literature it has shaped countless later authors in style and allusion. Each of these works was performed, recited, or read aloud long before it was studied in private, which helps explain their strong rhythms, repetitions, and memorable set pieces.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Who is Gilgamesh's companion, and what loss drives the hero's quest? 2) What is the central subject of the Iliad? 3) What does the Odyssey mainly follow? 4) Name two biblical books prized for their poetry. 5) What does reading the Bible 'as literature' emphasize? Answers: 1) Enkidu; his death sends Gilgamesh in search of immortality. 2) The wrath of Achilles during the Trojan War. 3) Odysseus' long journey home to Ithaca. 4) Any two of Psalms, Job, Song of Songs, Proverbs. 5) Its narrative, poetry, and imagery as crafted writing, rather than questions of doctrine.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling any long old book an 'epic'; the epic is specifically a long narrative poem of heroic action. Mistake: assuming Homer invented his stories alone, when he drew on a rich oral tradition. Mistake: thinking that reading scripture as literature denies or asserts its religious truth; it simply brackets that question to study the text's artistry. Exit ticket: (a) Which work is the oldest surviving epic? (b) What recurring theme links Gilgamesh and the Odyssey? Answers: (a) the Epic of Gilgamesh; (b) the hero's testing journey, and more broadly mortality, loss, and the longing to return or endure.

lessons.title: Classical Asia: Indian epics, Tang poetry, and The Tale of Genji
lessons.grammar_note: Transliterated names such as Li Bai and Du Fu keep their given order; do not reverse them into a Western first-name, last-name pattern.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to identify two towering Indian epics, two of China's greatest poets, and Japan's early prose masterpiece, and to say what each contributes to world literature. Warm-up: you have already named the author of The Tale of Genji in the diagnostic. What does it suggest about a culture when one of its earliest long works is a subtle novel of court life and feeling?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Classical Asia produced literature of enormous range and refinement. India's two great Sanskrit epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, blend adventure, ethics, and the sacred. The Ramayana follows the prince Rama, his wife Sita, and his effort to recover her from the demon king Ravana. The far longer Mahabharata recounts a dynastic war between the Pandavas and Kauravas and contains the Bhagavad Gita, a profound dialogue on duty between the warrior Arjuna and the god Krishna. In China, the Tang dynasty is remembered as a golden age of poetry, above all through Li Bai, famous for exuberant verse on wine, friendship, and the moon, and Du Fu, revered for compassionate, carefully wrought poems that register the suffering of his age. In Japan, Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji, written around the eleventh century, traces the loves and losses of a prince with psychological delicacy that still feels modern.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: The Ramayana is traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki; the Mahabharata to Vyasa, though both grew over centuries. Together they remain living texts, recited, performed, and retold across South and Southeast Asia. Li Bai (also written Li Po) and Du Fu, friends and contemporaries, are often paired as the two summits of Chinese poetry, the romantic and the moral realist. The Tale of Genji, by the court lady Murasaki Shikibu, is frequently called the world's first novel for its length, interiority, and unified narrative. These works show that the novel, the epic, and the lyric reached great heights in Asia, in some cases well before comparable European achievements.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Which Indian epic centers on Rama and the rescue of Sita? 2) In which epic does the Bhagavad Gita appear? 3) Name the two most celebrated Tang poets. 4) Who wrote The Tale of Genji, and roughly when? 5) Why is The Tale of Genji often called the first novel? Answers: 1) The Ramayana. 2) The Mahabharata. 3) Li Bai and Du Fu. 4) Murasaki Shikibu, around the eleventh century. 5) Because of its length, unified story, and deep attention to characters' inner lives.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the two Indian epics; remember Rama and Sita for the Ramayana, the Pandava-Kaurava war and the Gita for the Mahabharata. Mistake: treating Li Bai and Du Fu as interchangeable, when their voices differ sharply, one joyous and soaring, the other sober and humane. Mistake: assuming the novel is a purely European invention. Exit ticket: (a) Which epic contains the Bhagavad Gita? (b) What makes The Tale of Genji a candidate for the first novel? Answers: (a) the Mahabharata; (b) its sustained narrative length and rich psychological portrayal of its characters.

questions.prompt: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, whose death drives the hero to seek immortality?
questions.explanation: The loss of his companion Enkidu sends Gilgamesh in search of eternal life.

questions.prompt: The Iliad centers on the wrath of which Greek warrior during the Trojan War?
questions.explanation: The poem opens by naming the rage of Achilles and its terrible consequences.

questions.prompt: The Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue on duty, appears within which Indian epic?
questions.explanation: The Gita is set on the battlefield of the Mahabharata, between Arjuna and Krishna.

questions.prompt: The poets Li Bai and Du Fu belong to the golden age of poetry in which tradition?
questions.explanation: Both flourished during China's Tang dynasty.

questions.prompt: In the Ramayana, the prince Rama journeys to rescue his wife, who is named?
questions.explanation: Sita is carried off by the demon king Ravana, setting the epic's action in motion.

questions.prompt: Reading the Bible 'as literature' means attending mainly to?
options: its narratives, poetry, and imagery as a text
questions.explanation: The literary approach studies craft and artistry, bracketing questions of belief.

lessons.title: Medieval and early modern worlds: Dante to Shakespeare
lessons.grammar_note: Use 'medieval' for the roughly thousand-year span after antiquity and 'early modern' for the era of Cervantes and Shakespeare; the two labels are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to connect major works of the medieval and early modern periods across Europe and Asia, from Dante and the Thousand and One Nights to Cervantes, Shakespeare, and the classical theaters of China and Japan. Warm-up: you have already matched Scheherazade to her collection and Dante to his poem in the diagnostic. What might a frame story, a tale wrapped around other tales, let a writer do that a single straight narrative cannot?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The medieval world produced two works of lasting power from very different cultures. Dante's Divine Comedy sends its narrator through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, guided first by the Roman poet Virgil and then by his beloved Beatrice, building a vast moral and spiritual architecture in soaring Italian verse. The Arabic Thousand and One Nights frames a treasury of stories, Sindbad, Aladdin, Ali Baba, and more, inside the tale of Scheherazade, who postpones her execution night after night by never finishing a story. The early modern era then transformed prose and drama. Cervantes' Don Quixote, about a deluded knight and his earthy squire Sancho Panza, is often called the first modern novel. In England, Shakespeare reshaped tragedy and comedy in plays such as Hamlet and King Lear. Meanwhile East Asia developed rich theatrical traditions: Chinese drama from the Yuan plays to Tang Xianzu's Peony Pavilion, and Japanese Noh and the puppet and kabuki theater of Chikamatsu.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy in the early fourteenth century; it is a cornerstone of European literature and of the Italian language itself. The Thousand and One Nights grew over centuries from Arabic, Persian, and Indian sources and reached Europe in the eighteenth century, shaping how the West imagined storytelling. Miguel de Cervantes published Don Quixote in two parts (1605 and 1615). William Shakespeare, writing around 1600, remains the most performed and translated playwright in the world. In China, Tang Xianzu, a contemporary of Shakespeare, wrote the celebrated Peony Pavilion; in Japan, Zeami shaped Noh drama and Chikamatsu Monzaemon is sometimes called the Japanese Shakespeare for his puppet and kabuki plays.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Who guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory? 2) Who is the storyteller who frames the Thousand and One Nights? 3) Which work is often called the first modern novel, and who wrote it? 4) Name one Shakespeare tragedy. 5) Name one classical theater tradition of East Asia. Answers: 1) The Roman poet Virgil (Beatrice guides him in Paradise). 2) Scheherazade. 3) Don Quixote, by Cervantes. 4) Any of Hamlet, King Lear, Macbeth, Othello. 5) Any of Chinese Yuan or kunqu drama, Japanese Noh, kabuki, or puppet theater.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: blurring 'medieval' and 'early modern'; Dante is medieval, while Cervantes and Shakespeare are early modern. Mistake: thinking the Thousand and One Nights is a single authored book rather than a layered collection with a frame. Mistake: imagining great drama existed only in Europe, overlooking the sophisticated theaters of China and Japan. Exit ticket: (a) What is a frame story, in one sentence? (b) Which novel is widely regarded as the first modern one? Answers: (a) a narrative that encloses other stories within it, like Scheherazade's tales; (b) Cervantes' Don Quixote.

lessons.title: The novel's global rise and the shock of modernism
lessons.grammar_note: Realism and modernism name movements, not just moods; capitalize them only at the start of a sentence, and keep their meanings distinct.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain what the great realist novels achieved and how modernist writers then broke with them, and to name key figures on both sides of that shift. Warm-up: in the diagnostic you linked Flaubert, Kafka, and others to their movements. Think about one novel you know well: does it try to show life as it really is, or does it bend reality to capture a stranger truth? That tension is the heart of this lesson.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In the nineteenth century the novel became the dominant literary form, and realism its leading mode: the ambition to depict ordinary life, society, and inner experience with fidelity. In Russia, Leo Tolstoy built vast panoramas of history and marriage in War and Peace and Anna Karenina, while Fyodor Dostoevsky probed guilt, faith, and freedom in Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov. In France, Gustave Flaubert pursued precise, impersonal style in Madame Bovary. Then, early in the twentieth century, modernism unsettled these certainties. Writers questioned whether reality could be shown plainly at all, experimenting with time, perspective, and the uncanny. Franz Kafka turned anxiety and bureaucracy into nightmare parable in The Metamorphosis and The Trial. In Argentina, Jorge Luis Borges wrote short, dazzling fictions, labyrinths, libraries, and infinite books, that treat ideas themselves as adventures. Together these writers mark a turn from confident depiction to doubt, fragmentation, and play.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: Leo Tolstoy (War and Peace, Anna Karenina) and Fyodor Dostoevsky (Crime and Punishment, The Brothers Karamazov) are the giants of the Russian novel, one expansive and historical, the other intense and philosophical. Gustave Flaubert's Madame Bovary set a standard for stylistic exactness and became a landmark of realism. Franz Kafka, writing in German in Prague, left haunting works, many published after his death, whose adjective 'Kafkaesque' now names a whole kind of absurd, oppressive experience. Jorge Luis Borges, whose collections Ficciones and The Aleph reshaped the short story, influenced writers worldwide and helped prepare the ground for later experimental fiction. Across these authors you can watch the novel and story move from the mirror of realism toward the maze of modernism.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Name Flaubert's most famous novel and its movement. 2) What happens at the start of Kafka's Metamorphosis? 3) Which Dostoevsky novel follows the student Raskolnikov? 4) What kinds of images recur in Borges' fiction? 5) In one phrase, how does modernism differ from realism? Answers: 1) Madame Bovary; realism. 2) Gregor Samsa wakes transformed into a giant insect. 3) Crime and Punishment. 4) Labyrinths, libraries, mirrors, and infinite texts. 5) It doubts that reality can be shown plainly and experiments with form, time, and perspective.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using 'realism' loosely to mean 'realistic'; it names a deliberate nineteenth-century movement with its own aims. Mistake: treating Tolstoy and Dostoevsky as the same, when their styles and preoccupations differ. Mistake: thinking modernism simply abandoned meaning, when it often sought a deeper or stranger truth through new forms. Exit ticket: (a) Which movement prized faithful depiction of ordinary life? (b) Name one modernist writer and a hallmark of the work. Answers: (a) realism; (b) Kafka, whose fiction turns ordinary life into oppressive, dreamlike parable, or Borges, whose stories build intellectual labyrinths.

lessons.title: Postcolonial and twentieth-century voices
lessons.grammar_note: The adjective 'postcolonial' describes writing that responds to the legacy of empire; it is a critical term, not merely a date after independence.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to name major twentieth-century writers from Africa, Latin America, the Arab world, and South Asia, and explain how their work widened the map of world literature. Warm-up: in the diagnostic you identified Achebe's novel and the author of magical realism. Why does it matter that a global survey include voices writing from, and about, places long shaped by colonial rule?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The twentieth century brought a decisive broadening of world literature, as writers from formerly colonized regions and from traditions long underrepresented in the Western canon reached global audiences. In Nigeria, Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart told the story of the Igbo world and its disruption from the inside, answering centuries of outside depiction. In Colombia, Gabriel Garcia Marquez made the small town of Macondo a universe in One Hundred Years of Solitude, perfecting magical realism, in which the marvelous is reported in the same calm voice as the everyday. In Egypt, Naguib Mahfouz chronicled Cairo's families and streets across his Cairo Trilogy and many other works. In India, the poet and polymath Rabindranath Tagore wrote verse, fiction, drama, and song that bridged East and West. Different as they are, these writers share a drive to tell their own peoples' stories in their own terms, and to make local worlds speak to readers everywhere.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) is among the most widely read African novels and a foundational postcolonial text. Gabriel Garcia Marquez won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982, with One Hundred Years of Solitude as his best-known work. Naguib Mahfouz, who received the Nobel Prize in 1988, was the first Arabic-language writer to be so honored, celebrated for the Cairo Trilogy. Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913, the first from Asia, especially for Gitanjali, a collection of devotional poems. Reading these authors together shows world literature becoming genuinely worldwide, a conversation among many centers rather than one.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Who wrote Things Fall Apart, and about which people? 2) Which town is the setting of One Hundred Years of Solitude? 3) What style is Garcia Marquez famous for? 4) Which Egyptian writer wrote the Cairo Trilogy? 5) Who was the first Asian winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature? Answers: 1) Chinua Achebe, about the Igbo of Nigeria. 2) Macondo. 3) Magical realism. 4) Naguib Mahfouz. 5) Rabindranath Tagore, in 1913.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'postcolonial' as simply 'after independence'; it describes writing that engages with the legacy and aftermath of empire. Mistake: reducing magical realism to 'fantasy,' when its point is to narrate the marvelous as ordinary, often to express a particular cultural reality. Mistake: assuming world literature is mainly European, when much of its twentieth-century energy came from elsewhere. Exit ticket: (a) Define magical realism in one sentence. (b) Name one writer who helped bring a new region's voice into world literature. Answers: (a) a style that presents fantastic events in a matter-of-fact tone within an otherwise realistic world; (b) Achebe, Garcia Marquez, Mahfouz, or Tagore.

lessons.title: Great themes across traditions: the hero, the journey, love, and justice
lessons.grammar_note: A theme is an idea a work explores, such as justice; a plot is the sequence of events. Keep the two apart when you write about a book.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to trace a handful of great themes, the hero, the journey, love, and justice, across works from different cultures, and to use theme as a bridge between them. Warm-up: think back over the course so far. Which single idea seems to appear again and again, from Gilgamesh to the modern novel? Jot it down; you will likely find it among the four themes this lesson explores.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: One of the pleasures of world literature is seeing how different traditions take up the same deep human concerns. The hero, the figure who is tested and must grow or fall, appears as Gilgamesh, Achilles, Rama, Don Quixote, and in quieter form as the searching characters of modern novels. The journey, literal or inward, structures the Odyssey, the Divine Comedy, and countless stories of exile and return. Love, in its many shapes, from the courtly feeling of The Tale of Genji to the doomed passion of Anna Karenina, drives plots and reveals character everywhere. Justice, how a society defines and enforces right, animates Greek tragedy, the moral trials of Dostoevsky, and postcolonial novels that weigh the harms of conquest. Theme lets us compare without forcing works into a single mold: the same question, posed in many languages, draws out what each culture most values and fears.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: For the hero, set Gilgamesh and Achilles beside Rama and the self-deluding Don Quixote. For the journey, read the Odyssey next to Dante's Divine Comedy and the wanderings in the Thousand and One Nights. For love, compare the refined longing of Murasaki Shikibu's Genji with the destructive passion in Tolstoy's Anna Karenina. For justice, place the Mahabharata's debates on duty beside Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment and Achebe's portrait of a society under pressure in Things Fall Apart. None of these pairings erases differences; each sharpens them. Comparison by theme is a tool for seeing more clearly, not for declaring one tradition the winner.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Name two heroes from different cultures who are tested by hardship. 2) Which two works built around journeys could you fruitfully compare? 3) Give one work in which love drives the plot. 4) Name a work that wrestles with justice. 5) Why is theme a useful bridge between cultures? Answers: 1) Any two of Gilgamesh, Achilles, Rama, Don Quixote. 2) For example the Odyssey and the Divine Comedy. 3) Anna Karenina or The Tale of Genji. 4) Crime and Punishment, the Mahabharata, or Things Fall Apart. 5) Because the same human question, treated differently, reveals what each culture values.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing theme with plot; the theme is the idea explored, the plot is what happens. Mistake: using a shared theme to flatten real differences, as if all hero stories were the same. Mistake: forcing a theme onto a work it does not actually treat. Exit ticket: (a) In one sentence, what is a literary theme? (b) Name two of the four great themes surveyed here. Answers: (a) an idea or question a work explores, such as justice or love; (b) any two of the hero, the journey, love, and justice.

lessons.title: Applied task: compare two works across cultures

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will write a short comparative analysis of two works from different cultures, built around a single shared theme, and judge it against a clear rubric. This is the skill the whole course has been building toward: not just knowing works, but setting them side by side so that each illuminates the other. Warm-up: from the themes lesson, pick one idea, the hero, the journey, love, or justice, that genuinely connects two works you have met here.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A strong cross-cultural comparison does three things. First, it names a real point of contact, usually a shared theme, so the pairing is motivated rather than random. Second, it treats each work on its own terms, giving enough context that a reader unfamiliar with one or both can follow. Third, and most important, it uses the comparison to reveal something neither work shows alone: a difference in values, form, or outcome that only emerges in the pairing. Avoid the trap of mere summary, retelling both plots and stopping there, and avoid ranking, declaring one work 'better' because it is more familiar. The goal is insight. A useful structure is: state the shared theme and your claim; present the first work briefly; present the second; then devote your strongest paragraphs to the comparison itself, where you argue what the contrast means.

sections.heading: Key works & authors
sections.text: You have a wide field to choose from. For the journey, you might pair Homer's Odyssey with Dante's Divine Comedy, or either with the wanderings in the Thousand and One Nights. For the hero, set the Epic of Gilgamesh beside the Ramayana, or Achilles beside Don Quixote. For love, compare The Tale of Genji with Anna Karenina. For justice, place Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment beside Achebe's Things Fall Apart, or the Mahabharata's debates on duty beside a modern novel. Pick two works you can discuss with some specificity, from genuinely different traditions, so that the comparison has real distance to cross.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Task: in about 300 words, compare two works from different cultures through one shared theme, following the three-part structure above. Here is a short model to show the tone and moves, not to copy. 'Both the Odyssey and Dante's Divine Comedy are journeys, yet they travel in opposite directions. Odysseus struggles outward and homeward across a dangerous sea, driven by longing for Ithaca, family, and the ordinary life he lost. Dante's pilgrim travels inward and upward through the afterlife, driven by longing for understanding and for Beatrice. Homer's journey restores a man to the world; Dante's lifts him beyond it. Read together, they suggest two ancient answers to the same question, what is the journey for: one points home, the other points to heaven. The contrast shows how a Greek epic prizes return and human community, while a medieval Christian poem prizes ascent and the soul's destination.' Notice that the model names the theme, treats each work fairly, and spends its energy on what the contrast reveals.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Now grade your own draft with this self-check rubric. Answer yes to each: (1) I named one shared theme and a clear claim before comparing. (2) I gave enough context on each work for an outside reader to follow. (3) I spent more words on the comparison than on summary. (4) I showed what the contrast reveals about each culture or work, rather than ranking them. (5) My prose is my own, not copied from the model. If all five are yes, you have written a real comparative analysis. Common mistakes to watch for: summarizing both works and never comparing; choosing two works so alike that the comparison is flat; and smuggling in a verdict about which tradition is 'superior.'
